item.title: Divide among BRICs nations exposed as Houthi rebels seize oil chokepoint in Red Sea
item.description: The New Delhi declaration has no mention of the issue which expands Iran’s control leaving Saudi Arabia exposed, though both countries are part of the grouping.
item.content:encoded:
Houthi rebel forces have seized the Yemeni port of Mokha as well as Mayyun Island overlooking the Bab el-Mandab strait. This gives Iran’s most powerful remaining proxy force in the Middle East nearly complete control of Yemen’s entire Red Sea coast.

Directly or indirectly, Tehran now has a chokehold on around 12% of global trade that passes through that waterway. It is also maintaining its pressure on the Strait of Hormuz, which has already led to a cut of flows there from about 9 million barrels of oil a day to between 3.7 and 6.4 million.

The day after the Houthis took control of the Bab al-Mandab Strait, Brics leaders assembled in New Delhi, for their 18th annual summit. Brics is the group of “emerging economies” which formed around Brazil, Russia, India, China, and South Africa in 2006, to counter western influence in global institutions. It has since added six permanent members: Egypt, Ethiopia, Iran, Saudi Arabia, UAE and Indonesia. A further ten countries, Belarus, Bolivia, Kazakhstan, Cuba, Malaysia, Nigeria, Thailand, Uganda, Uzbekistan and Vietnam joined as “partner countries” in 2025.

item.title: Muslim man detained on suspicion of being undocumented Bangladeshi released from Bengal jail
item.description: Jalil Akhtar was picked up from his home in June and the police made at least one attempt to deport him, despite his family submitting land records from 1967.
item.content:encoded:
A Muslim man who had been detained on suspicion of being an undocumented Bangladeshi citizen and sent to a detention centre in June was released from jail on Tuesday, his cousin told Scroll.

Jalil Akhtar, a resident of Uttar Dinajpur district in West Bengal, secured bail on Monday, his cousin Matiur Rahman said.

He had been picked up from his home on June 19. His family had told Scroll that there was no basis for police to suspect that he was a Bangladeshi citizen. They said Akhtar’s name appeared in the electoral rolls prepared after the special intensive revision in both 2002 and 2026.

Since he was detained, the police made at least one attempt to deport him, according to a report filed by the Dalkhola police in the Uttar Dinajpur court on August 1.

Akhtar was kept at a temporary holding centre in Nizampur “and all biometric and deportation formalities were completed”, the report said. He was handed over to the Border Security Force on July 4 and asked to be deported.

Having failed to force him out, the police had filed a suo moto case against him under the Immigration and Foreigners Act, 2025, alleging that he had entered the country without a valid passport, travel document or visa.

item.title: Graham Staines murder: Odisha denies early release to convict
item.description: Bajrang Dal member Dara Singh’s release could lead to communal disturbance, the state sentence review board held.
item.content:encoded:
The Odisha government has rejected the early release of Bajrang Dal member Dara Singh, who is serving a life sentence for the 1999 murder of Australian missionary Graham Staines and his two sons, PTI reported on Tuesday.

The director general of prisons and correctional services and the authorities at Kendujhar Jail had earlier recommended his release on grounds of good behaviour. Singh has spent more than 26 years in prison.

At a meeting on August 31, the state sentence review board decided against Singh’s early release noting that it could lead to communal disturbance in the area, The Hindu reported.

The board also stated that on August 15, a group of around 200-250 persons associated with Dara Sena had assembled outside the Kendujhar district jail in connection with the proposed release of the convict, during which “provocative slogans” were shouted, the newspaper reported.

Dara Sena – named after Singh – is an outfit that campaigns for his release.

In a 2024 remission plea before the Supreme Court, Singh argued that he should be considered for early release as he was above 60 and had spent more than 24 years in prison. item.title: In India, nicotine pouches are slipping through regulatory cracks
item.description: The marketing of these products is aimed at young people. But the WHO has warned that nicotine is addictive and could affect brain development of teenagers.
item.content:encoded:
There’s a new menace in town, thanks to an “innovation” by Big Tobacco.

A new study led by Indian Medical Research Council’s National Institute of Cancer Prevention and Research has found that oral nicotine pouches are reaching Indian cities through online platforms, hookah shops and gig delivery services even though it is not clear which Indian law – if any – governs these addictive, tobacco-free sachets are governed.

They are available in 445 flavours, at strengths of up to 120 mg.

The report warns that such pouches are an emerging public-health risk in India. They are rapidly penetrating urban markets and targeting youth through regulatory blind spots.

A nicotine pouch is a small, tobacco-free, tea-bag-like sack containing nicotine, flavorings, and plant-based fibres. Users tuck the pouch between their lip and gum for up to an hour, allowing nicotine to be absorbed directly into the bloodstream without smoke, vapour or spitting.

The Indian report followed a warning from the World Health Organization in May about the dangers posed by nicotine pouches. These products are already banned in several countries, including Singapore, France, Belgium and the Netherlands.

item.title: Fiction: A college lecturer is caught in the machinery of state repression during the Emergency
item.description: An excerpt from ‘Diary of an Unseen Witness’, by Ampassayya Naveen, translated from the Telugu by Kalpana Kannabiran.
item.content:encoded:
June 20, 1976

It is night, around 2 am I just can’t sleep. I could hear the sound of a drizzle outside, but it was sultry inside the house. I tossed about in bed. Suseela, and my younger boy, Sudheer were fast asleep. The other two children were peacefully asleep in another cot.

I wondered a couple of times whether I should wake Suseela up. She seemed to be in a deep sleep. Why wake her? I lit a cigarette and lay back thinking.

On 25th June last year, the country was enveloped in the darkness of an eclipse. Anticipation of something to come… tension…disquiet…fear…disturbance.

I learnt later that on 26th, Venu and several revolutionary writers had been arrested in Warangal. They also searched for Rammohan the same day. But Rammohan had gone underground by then. Around that time, colleagues from my staff room, informed me, “There is an enquiry being conducted on you. Be careful.” Those words made my heart sink.

“Why me? What did I do?” I asked.

“You didn’t do anything. What did the people who are being arrested do?” they replied.

item.title: Canada deports four Indians in extortion crackdown
item.description: More than 100 foreign citizens had been deported and 188 were issued a removal notice as of September 3 for alleged links to organised crime and violence.
item.content:encoded:
Canada has deported four Indians in an immigration crackdown targeting foreign citizens allegedly linked to extortion groups, the country’s border services agency said on Monday.

The deportations were part of a law enforcement campaign against persons with alleged links to criminal organisations targeting South Asian businesses and families in Alberta, British Columbia and Ontario.

The agency said that it had issued 188 removal orders and deported 111 persons by September 3 as part of the crackdown. Fifty of the orders were issued to persons in the Greater Toronto Area, and 23 individuals in the region had been deported.

Amitoz Bajwa, Jasmer Singh, Palwinder Singh and Sahibjot Singh were deported after they were found inadmissible under Canada’s Immigration and Refugee Protection Act.

Palwinder Singh was removed from the country after the Immigration and Refugee Board of Canada found him inadmissible under the Act for being a member of a criminal group linked to extortion-related violence, the border services agency said.

Jasmer Singh, convicted in Canada for forcible confinement, was found inadmissible for serious criminality, the agency said.

item.content:encoded:
The Delhi High Court on Monday granted bail to a man who had spent eight years in jail after being arrested under the Unlawful Activities Prevention Act in 2018, reported Bar and Bench.

Noting that only 40 out of 120 witnesses have been examined by the prosecution so far, a bench of Justices Navin Chawla and Ravinder Dudeja said it was “moved, particularly by the long period of incarceration”, reported ANI.

“We are of the opinion that the appellant has been able to make out a case for being released on bail,” the bench held.

The man, Mohammad Saqib, had been arrested in December 2018 under the Unlawful Activities Prevention Act, the Explosive Substances Act and the Indian Penal Code.

item.title: Bengal withdraws approval for Akshaya Patra Foundation to provide mid-day meals in 4 districts
item.description: While the government did not specify a reason for the decision, heads of several schools flagged difficulties in serving boiled eggs separately to students.
item.content:encoded:
The West Bengal government has withdrawn its approval for the ISKCON-linked Akshaya Patra Foundation to supply mid-day meals to schools in four districts, reported The Indian Express on Tuesday.

The foundation had been given approval to provide the meals to schools in Howrah, Purulia, North 24 Parganas and Purba Medinipur through an order issued on August 21.

On September 11, Paromita Roy, the joint secretary of the State Education Department, rescinded the order without specifying any reason, the newspaper reported.

The heads of several schools said that arrangements had not been made for the foundation to supply cooked meals in the districts, reported The Times of India. They also flagged difficulties in providing boiled eggs separately to students, as was being done in schools in Kolkata.

It is unclear whether the Akshaya Patra Foundation had said it would exclude eggs from the mid-day meals in the four districts. She and the organisations have been protesting against the Siang Multipurpose Project, a proposed 12,500-megawatt power project on Arunachal Pradesh’s Siang river. The organisation Dibang resistance has also been protesting against a 2,880-megawatt power project on the Dibang river.

item.title: This book examines nonbinary thinking and Christianity in the late Roman Empire and the Middle Ages
item.description: An excerpt from ‘Humans: A Monstrous History’, by Surekha Davies.
item.content:encoded:
Between late antiquity and the end of the Middle Ages (ca. 200–1400 CE), Christian scholars, theologians, jurists, and medical practitioners frequently drew on the Bible to think and write about nonbinary individuals. At stake was figuring out the limits of who counted as human – and, by extension, who got to go to heaven (sins permitting). The Book of Genesis contains a potential nonbinary individual at the start of human history: Adam.

God was said to have created Adam and then created Eve. According to some early versions of Genesis, God split Adam in half, using one of his sides to make Eve. In a translated version that became widespread, Eve was created from Adam’s rib (and was therefore, by implication, inferior to Adam). Either way, for some early Christian thinkers, Adam may have begun as a unified whole transcending the male/female division. Medieval science and gender historian Leah DeVun and other scholars of early Christianity call this idea “primal androgyny.”

Adam’s potential androgyny raised troubling questions for adherents of gender binaries in the here and now: Was the original “natural” state of humans androgyny (the absence of sex), or did human history begin at some point after that, once Eve was created...

item.description: Some social media accounts had criticised the officer for using Islamic greetings in a social media video instead of saying ‘Vande Mataram’ or ‘Jai Hind’.
item.content:encoded:
Indian Police Service officer Bushara Bano was transferred by the West Bengal government on Monday, two days after Hindutva groups criticised for using Islamic greetings in a video posted online, The Times of India reported.

In the video posted on Sunday, Bano had spoken about how the Residential Coaching Academy of the Aligarh Muslim University in Uttar Pradesh had helped her prepare for the Union Public Service Commission exam.

Some social media accounts including The Jaipur Dialogue and the Hindu Legal Fund, had criticised the Muslim IPS officer for saying “assalamualaikum”, a greeting that means “peace be unto you”, as well as “inshallah”, a phrase meaning god willing, and “jazakallah”, which means “may god reward you”.

They said that she had not said “Vande Mataram” or “Jai Hind”.

“A serving officer representing the Indian state should maintain neutrality and use national expressions in public communication,” The Hindu Legal Fund had said.

The group said that it had filed a complaint with the West Bengal home secretary and sought action.

item.title: US judge blocks Trump’s new rules limiting visa duration for students, journalists
item.description: A day before the rules were to take effect, the court said that Washington was adopting the policy based on ‘exceptionally weak’ rationales.
item.content:encoded:
A federal judge in the United States on Monday blocked the Donald Trump administration from implementing a new rule that would limit how long foreign students and journalists can remain in the US without applying to extend their visas, Reuters reported.

The judge ruled in favour of unions and higher education advocacy groups a day before the new rules were scheduled to take effect.

In July, the Trump administration had announced the new rules, under which international students would only be able to remain in the country for a maximum of four years. The changes would curb “visa abuse”, the Department of Homeland Security had said.

Since 1978, foreign students, or F visa holders, could stay in the US for their “duration of status” or as long as they were enrolled as a full-time student.

The new rule would impact visitors on cultural exchange programmes who possess a J visa and international journalists with an I visa. The visa for members of the media will be limited to 240 days.

These visas are currently available for the duration of an educational programme or employment in the US.

item.title: In India, the battle to love and the fundamental right to making a family
item.description: Appreciating choices made out of love can build enduring legacies. Others instead just live with ideas of honour and regret.
item.content:encoded:
I attended a beautiful church wedding in Mumbai’s Bandra neighbourhood with music and dance, a white wedding gown and a three-tiered cake. The bride, a Marathi woman from an Other Backward Classes, was marrying a Goan Catholic man who was her classmate in college. She was an accomplished woman and practising chartered accountant.

Watching everyone dance and sip wine, I was delighted and intrigued. “How did you accept her choice so easily?” I asked her parents. “You have never met Christians before! Did you not worry?”

They responded, “What is the point of raising children to be independent and intelligent, if you cannot trust their decisions? By being negative, you will just lose your children. We are not that stupid.”

Sadly, many parents are. When my cousin and his girlfriend declared their intent to marry, her father was very upset. “You have so many male friends, why do you choose to marry this Muslim guy?” he said. “That other fellow – surname Kamath – he could be as good surely!”

item.title: A new book recounts events leading up to the first Kashmir war fought immediately after Partition
item.description: An excerpt from ‘1947: The Battle of Badgam and Shalateng’, by Ajay Kumar Raina with Shiv Kunal Verma.
item.content:encoded:
By the late summer of 1947, Jammu and Kashmir was already under sustained pressure, well before the first tribal columns crossed its borders. The deterioration of security within the state did not occur in isolation, nor was it confined to communal unrest. It was the outcome of a coordinated process in which political mobilisation, economic strangulation, and covert military preparation converged to weaken the state from within and render it vulnerable to external assault.

The pattern of instability was geographically uneven. While the Kashmir Valley and Ladakh remained relatively calm through August and September 1947, conditions in Jammu Province deteriorated rapidly. The violence that accompanied the Partition in Punjab spilled across the border, particularly after the announcement of the Punjab Boundary Award on August 17. Refugees fleeing attacks in West Punjab, especially from the Hazara district, poured into Jammu in large numbers, overwhelming administrative capacity and fuelling cycles of reprisal and counter-reprisal.

This instability was neither accidental nor self-contained. Even as communal tensions escalated, political and military mobilisation against the state was already underway. item.title: UPI charges of 0.4% on merchant transactions above Rs 2,000
item.description: Banks have been advised to ensure that the charges are not passed on to the customers, the Ministry of Finance said.
item.content:encoded:
The Union government on Monday clarified that Unified Payments Interface transactions to merchants valued above Rs 2,000 will attract a fee of 0.4%.

“Banks have been advised to ensure that merchants do not pass Merchant discount rate charges on to customers,” the Ministry of Finance said. “Application providers are expressly prohibited from imposing platform fees or hidden charges.”

Merchant discount rate is a fee charged to businesses by banks to cover the costs of processing transactions. The rate typically ranges from 1% to 3% of the transaction value for credit card payments and can be up to 0.9% for debit card transactions.

This 0.4% fee has been capped at Rs 300 per transaction for payments of Rs 75,000 and above.

The ministry said that the new framework will have no impact on person-to-person transactions, “irrespective of the amount transferred”.

item.description: Around 1,200 families living around Kuno National Park will be uprooted by the project.

In April, an Indian-born cheetah, KP-2, walked several hundred kilometres from Kuno National Park in Madhya Pradesh to Rajasthan’s Ranthambore National Park.

KP-2’s mother, Asha, was one of eight cheetahs brought to Kuno from Namibia in September 2022, as a part of India’s cheetah reintroduction project. Today, there are a total of 48 cheetahs in the country, including 28 Indian-born cubs – most of them, however, remain in enclosures in Kuno. Three are roaming free in Gandhi Sagar Wildlife Sanctuary in Madhya Pradesh, which was developed as a second site for the cheetahs.

item.title: AI has made it harder to find reliable information
item.description: Many websites are blocking scraping tools while AI results now depend more on low-quality websites.
item.content:encoded:
For 30 years, the world wide web has run on a surprisingly profound social contract: most sites are free for search engines to access, but if you use their content you give credit by linking to the source.

Recently, that social contract has begun to collapse. Artificial intelligence (AI) tools are crawling sites not to link to them, but to train models and generate answers (which may or may not be accurate).

When you search for something, ChatGPT’s response or Google’s AI Overviews may still include links to sources, but they’re a kind of optional extra to the main answer.

This has triggered a bad dynamic for website owners, the public, and even AI companies themselves: as websites lose traffic (and revenue), many are beginning to block AI scraping tools, meaning AI results depend more on low-quality websites (many of which are also generated by AI). As a result, good information can be harder than ever to find.

How we got here

In the early days of the world wide web, search engines and content creators came to an agreement about crawling (the practice of technologically examining a site to index it, so it can be served up in search results). item.title: ‘Deviously devoid of all language’: Five poems on the absurdity of suffering and the cosmic machine
item.description: An excerpt from ‘Night breaks apart, like pomegranate seeds in my palm’, by Aakriti Kuntal.
item.content:encoded:
Evening

Evening,
a marble plateau,
sliced breath of the day

Red pomegranate seeds splutter,
turning the mouth’s estranged sky
into a velvet sienna

Stillness—
lack of movement
or lack of thought?

An elongation of emotion
a requiem for the living

The air, it seems,
is suffused with a flat, ochre light,
static around the bark of all trees

A consolation,
a lullaby,
a long, long pause
everything in the goddamn world
bending down
to stare at its very own miracle

Twilight’s veil flutters,
an insect strapped to the day’s chest

She moves,

Slowly,
Carefully—
there are no mistakes made here
the day falls in precise moments,
just as it began

A cold shudder

A celestial beast
salivates over life’s porous face

And the horizon grins

Evening,
the sly tongue of light


Lilith

Lilith,
sepulcher of stunted air

A thin laugh—
the drooping Venus-tongues
ecstatic in the wedges of space

My garden blistered with their warm breath,
their constant heaving

Their inaudible, glaring presence
thousands of purple baby-fists

Hanging, just
hanging

The most precious of sights

yet appalling,
very appalling

Lilith,
your large, viscous being
above these pockets of breasts

You stand
with your tongue deep in my mouth,
a fine straw of divine ache

You stand—still,
deviously devoid of all language,

You stand,
seeking neither forgiveness
nor awaiting any,

You stand outside,
outside breath, sense, being,

You stand,
outside of all human judgement—
plain vicious,

the glorious face of luscious lunacy


Abduction

White salt out there,
your whitewashed twigs scowl—

motions unfamiliar

The night is growing thick;
the finger is aflame, a matchstick

It has sworn to shimmer;
the teeth abandon the jaw
and float into the sea,

A jawbone into the sea’s eternity
a poet stood before the ocean

And never returned,
return he did not

a quarter of the moon, the man’s weakening

item.title: Retail inflation rises to 4.8%, wholesale inflation to 9.9% in August
item.description: The wholesale inflation has also been rising since the beginning of the financial year because of the war in West Asia.
item.content:encoded:
India’s retail inflation rose to 4.8% in August from 4.4% in July, and the wholesale price inflation increased to 9.9% from 9.7%, according to government data released on Monday.

Retail inflation measures the change in consumer prices in a month on a year-on-year basis.

The wholesale price index tracks the average changes in prices of a basket of goods that are sold in bulk before they make their way to retail consumers. The base year for calculating wholesale price index is 2022-’23.

The rise in retail inflation was largely driven by higher food prices. Food inflation increased to 5.9% in August from 5.5% in July, according to the National Statistics Office.

Prices of staples such as ginger, onion and garlic rose sharply. Inflation in food-serving services also increased to 8.4% from 7.7%. The transport inflation rose to 4.6% from 4.4%.

The wholesale inflation has also been rising since the beginning of the financial year because of the war in West Asia and the resulting blockade of the Strait of Hormuz, PTI reported. India imports 88% of its crude oil and about half of its natural gas, much of it through the strait.

The disruption has also had a spillover effect on food prices.

Nations that controlled islands where spices were grown were extremely protective of their crops. The Dutch, above all, were highly sensitive about protection. To stop their nutmeg from being reseeded, they covered this export crop with lime. The Dutch also set their clove groves on fire both to control the market and to keep others from getting a new crop from the plants. China “significantly reduced” its Army deployment along India’s northern borders in 2025, the Ministry of Defence has said in its annual report.

However, 10 combined arms brigade-size forces remain deployed in areas along the Line of Actual Control and in traditional training areas, the ministry said in its report for the financial year 2025-’26. Each brigade of this size typically comprises about 5,000 personnel, according to independent analysts.

Border tensions between India and China escalated in June 2020 when a violent face-off between Indian and Chinese soldiers took place in Ladakh’s Galwan Valley along the Line of Actual Control. It led to the deaths of 20 Indian soldiers. Beijing said that the clash left four of its soldiers dead.

Following the face-off, both countries deployed thousands of soldiers along with heavy artillery in the region.

Since the Galwan clashes, China and India have held several rounds of military and diplomatic talks to resolve their border standoff.

In October 2024, the two countries announced that they had reached a patrolling arrangement along the Line of Actual Control, “leading to the disengagement” of the two militaries in eastern Ladakh.

Khatun had returned to her home in Bengal’s Murshidabad district from Kolkata shortly after midnight.

Around 12.30 am, she was in bed, when a group of men knocked on the door of their home in Ramakantapur village.

“They called out my father-in-law’s name,” Khatun said.

When 61-year-old Ibrahim Sheikh opened the door, Khatun said, a group of seven or eight men surrounded him. They were in civilian clothes but Khatun said they appeared to be police officials.

“They demanded to see his documents and so he showed them his Aadhaar and voter cards,” Khatun said. “Then, they asked him, ‘Aapni ki Indian, na Bangaldeshi?’” Are you Indian or Bangladeshi?

Sheikh asserted that he was Indian, not Bangladeshi, Khatun said. But the men said they had information that Sheikh was not an Indian citizen.

They went on to grab Sheikh from behind, Khatun said. As they roughed him up, pinning his hands at the back, he became “very afraid” and “agreed with whatever the police were saying”.

item.title: Eating a serving of nuts can help lower risk of hypertension, say researchers
item.description: Plant foods share a few key characteristics, which may explain why they’re beneficial for the heart.
item.content:encoded:
More than 1.4 billion people worldwide live with high blood pressure (hypertension). It’s the single biggest metabolic risk factor for early death – driving diseases such as heart attacks, strokes, kidney failure and dementia.

Most of these cases of high blood pressure are shaped by how we live and what we eat. This means that making changes to your diet can have a big impact on your risk of developing high blood pressure.

Even small changes can help, as our latest research shows. We found that adding just one serving of nuts into your daily diet is linked with lower hypertension risk.

It’s well known that eating more plant foods is associated with a lower risk of hypertension – but research on the impact of nuts has been limited to date.

Fruits and vegetables are associated with a lower risk of hypertension, with consumption of 800g (ten portions) per day reducing the risk by 11%.

Whole grains – brown rice, oats, wholemeal bread – are similarly linked to lower risk of hypertension. Our research found that the people who consumed the highest amount of whole grains each day had a roughly 26% lower risk compared to people consuming the least.

item.description: The code is in force in Uttarakhand. Gujarat, Assam and Madhya Pradesh await assent, while Maharashtra, West Bengal, Chhattisgarh and Rajasthan are drafting it.
item.content:encoded:
Union Home Minister Amit Shah on Sunday said that governments led by the Bharatiya Janata Party and its National Democratic Alliance partners in all 21 states would introduce the Uniform Civil Code before 2029.

The next Lok Sabha elections are scheduled for 2029.

“We have introduced the Uniform Civil Code in several states and I am confident that in the 21 BJP-NDA ruled states, we will introduce the UCC before 2029,” Shah said, while speaking about the Union government’s achievements over the past 12 years.

The Uniform Civil Code aims to introduce a common set of laws governing marriage, divorce, succession and adoption for all citizens. Currently, such personal affairs of different religions are based on community-specific laws, largely derived from religious scripture.

Introducing a common personal law has for long been on the BJP’s agenda and several states ruled by the party have been making advances towards implementing it.

In January 2025, Uttarakhand became the first state to implement the Uniform Civil Code after Independence when it brought the code into force. Gujarat, Assam and Madhya Pradesh have passed similar legislations but are awaiting presidential assent and notification, Hindustan Times reported.

The Maharashtra, West Bengal and Chhattisgarh governments have formed committees to draft Uniform Civil Codes. The Rajasthan Cabinet also approved a bill to introduce such a legislation in August.

item.title: ‘Notes on the Rock of Job Charnock’: Kolkata emerges as a site of psychic inheritance in these poems
item.description: Poet Jaydeep Sarangi also sustains the marginal voices and their subjective histories that modernity’s enlightenment project tends to disregard.
item.content:encoded:
Celebrated as the “Bard on the Banks of Dulung”, Jaydeep Sarangi, the prolific writer and poet from Jhargram, has a reputation that is indeed formidable. A significant portion of his scholarship examines themes within Indian Writing in English, Dalit marginalised literatures, postcolonial studies, and translation studies. Rather than employing the city trope as a glorious spectacle or a site of ruin, Sarangi’s recent poetry collection, Notes on the Rock of Job Charnock treats it as a palimpsest of time, following a fascinating yet distinctly subversive trajectory. As a disavowal of the grand meta-narratives of history, it lends itself to a multilayered civilisational memory, with all its nuances, to cull out a truly personal reflection of individual memory.

Sarangi’s novel poetic expression sustains fragile experiences of subjectivity against the erosions of time and memory. Embedded in culture and mnemonic sites, the poems trace the umpteen historical layers – in the city’s rivers, ghats, myths, and marginalised existences. And yet, above all, it remains a personal archive of recollection. The Kolkata evoked in these poems is animated by liminality, in which one witnesses the convergence of emotion, history, and spirituality.

item.title: ‘Under Water’: Tara Menon’s fragmented debut on grief and climate change never quite comes together
item.description: The novel has a clear thesis about grief and climate change, but its scattered, trivia-heavy prose keeps it from proving it.
item.content:encoded:
When the reader meets Marissa, the protagonist of Tara Menon’s Under Water, all that could happen to her has already happened. The banality of a new, if lax, life taxes her. A home awaits her – one she surely misses. She cannot fathom returning, though. It was in Thailand that a ravenous tsunami had gulped down Arielle, her once-infallible friend.

Six-year-old Arielle, upon meeting a freshly motherless Marissa, asserts that they can share hers. From then on, they share everything. They slice open a watermelon and eat it whole. Their teeth sink into fridge-cold mangoes. They bite into piping-hot pa thong ko slathered in condensed milk. They chug stolen bottles of Bacardi Breezers. For all their shared endeavours, what these two friends don’t seem to share is conversation; their banter is often laconic, even if the narration insists otherwise. No wonder, then, that Arielle, a literal apparition in half of the novel, is a literary apparition in the other. By the time she dies her inevitable death, I know her even less. Why did the hen cross the road?

For freedom, adventure and meaning.

The black-coloured hen with a crimson comb and piercing yellow eyes flees the coop at first chance. Later found and tended to by an elderly man, the hen produces a series of eggs that are inevitably taken away. The hen uses its bird brain to figure out an escape plan. It bears witness to an immigrant trafficking racket. It encounters compassion and cruelty in equal measure.

There is dust.

They are endless.

Did I mention dust?

The British Library. Big, Brutalist, red-bricked, stone-paved, and in one corner, perpetually in attendance, Paolozzi’s naked Newton hunched over a pair of dividers. item.title: AI in election governance technology should be a global concern

In July, all 193 United Nations member states gathered in Geneva for the inaugural Global Dialogue on AI Governance. For two days they debated how the world should govern AI, yet paid little attention to one of AI’s most consequential governance challenges: its impact on elections. The omission risks undermining progress on every other aspect of the AI debate: safety, trustworthiness, capacity building, societal implications, and human rights.

Elections are not simply another sector affected by AI; they are the main mechanism that makes every other democratic right enforceable. Yet when we think about AI and elections, many of us think about disinformation. item.content:encoded:
East Africa’s shrinking mountain glaciers on three peaks in Kenya, Uganda and Tanzania will soon be no more. The 2025 State of the Climate in Africa report (page 13) estimates that the ice areas on Mt Kenya, the continent’s second-highest peak, have shrunk 96% in the past 115 years. The ice cap will cease to exist in three to five years, says the report. Rainer Prinz, who studies climate-glacier relationships, explains the intricate processes behind the retreat and what the consequences will be.

What makes up the ice caps?

Glacier ice consists of snow accumulated over decades and centuries. Some snow may melt during summer or warm seasons. But some remains and is covered by more snow falling during the wet seasons. Glacier ice, which makes up the bulk of the white mountain tops, is formed by this process.

There are glaciers on Mt Kenya, Kilimanjaro in northern Tanzania and Rwenzori, on the border between Uganda and the Democratic Republic of Congo.

These glaciers have increased and decreased in size during the past centuries and millennia following wetter and drier climatic conditions. The glaciers as features might be as old as 10,000 years, but the ice itself is considerably younger.

The current glacier retreat is unprecedented, outside the range of its natural variation....

item.title: Telangana’s tiger reserve with no tigers
item.description: The Kawal Tiger Reserve connects major tiger landscapes and has large prey populations but no resident big cats.
item.content:encoded:
Deep in northern Telangana, Kawal Tiger Reserve covers a thick forest of teak and bamboo near the Godavari river. Geographically, it sits in an ideal location, connecting major tiger landscapes. It links Tadoba-Andhari in Maharashtra to the west and Indravati in Chhattisgarh to the east. Kawal supports large populations of spotted deer, sambar, nilgai, and wild pigs, alongside leopards and wild dogs. On paper, the tiger reserve checks the boxes of sufficient prey and habitat. But the reserve has no resident tigers.

A 12-year study conducted between 2010 and 2022 confirmed that no tigers live permanently in Kawal. Using systematically placed line transects to monitor prey numbers, researchers found that spotted deer populations grew over the decade, while sambar, nilgai, and chousingha populations remained stable.

Despite this rich prey base, researchers recorded only 15 transient tigers entering Kawal from Maharashtra since 2015. Crucially, only two of these visiting tigers were female. While neighbouring corridors outside the reserve have breeding tigers with cubs, Kawal itself remains empty.

The astonishing true story of Thomas Cochrane – naval hero, political radical and inspiration for Patrick O’Brian’s Jack Aubrey – whose audacity at sea, scandals on land and battles across empires make for a tale as thrilling as any novel.

Cochrane’s life was even more remarkable than the fiction it inspired. A hero of the Napoleonic Wars, known for destroying the French Atlantic fleet in one explosive attack, he was an equally aggressive force in British politics as the radical MP for Westminster.

Cochrane’s fortunes turned in 1814, when he was convicted of a fraud on the Stock Exchange. After escaping from prison, he later reinvented himself as a revolutionary admiral, helping the Chileans, Peruvians, Brazilians and Greeks in their struggles for independence.

item.description: Rejimon Kuttappan’s novel has its poignant moments, but they are needles in its haystack of digression and awkward prose.

Reading The River of Grey Flowers feels a lot like watching Dhurandhar. While Rejimon Kuttappan’s debut novel has none of Aditya Dhar’s right-wing nationalism, it succumbs to the same fatal flaw in narrative: it depends so much on its events being true stories that it fails to create enough stakes for the characters within its fiction.

The circumstances

Kuttappan is an investigative journalist specialising in migrant rights and forced labour, and this novel borrows from much of the news he has broken. It follows John Easow, a Dalit fisherman’s son, who is a graphic designer by day and turmeric smuggler by night. When he falls in love with Thenmozhi, a savarna woman from the neighbouring village, they marry in secret; he is forced to give up his boat, and therefore his income from smuggling, in exchange for his life. item.title: How India opened a consulate in Odessa – and why it took years
item.description: The mission was meant to serve India’s growing trade with the Soviet Union, but it soon became a hub for sailors, students and cultural exchange.
item.content:encoded:
When Indian foreign service officer PH Desai inaugurated his country’s consulate in Odessa in November 1962, the Black Sea port greeted the milestone with much fanfare. At the time, only three foreign governments maintained diplomatic missions anywhere in the Soviet Union outside Moscow: fellow communist nations Poland and Czechoslovakia operated consulates in Kiev, while Turkey had one in Batumi.

Local journalists covered the opening in a city celebrated for its 19th-century maritime legacy and scarred by fierce fighting during the Second World War. Addressing the press at the opening, Desai noted that three Indian companies maintained regular shipping services between Odessa and Indian ports, while vessels of the Black Sea Shipping Line frequently called at Indian ports.

Odessa carried immense strategic value for New Delhi as the port from where machinery and equipment for the expansion of the Bhilai Steel Plant were shipped to India. In the preceding decade, the absence of an on-the-ground Indian mission had created headaches. Indian merchant seamen frequently attempted to disembark during port calls, leading to tensions, as embassy files from Moscow note, when local authorities refused a few of them entry into the Soviet Union.

item.title: Size matters: Why India has a stake in the Africa-led campaign to decolonise world maps
item.description: The Mercator map that is now most familiar distorts the size of Africa, Latin America, South Asia and Oceania and inflates landmasses towards the poles.
item.content:encoded:
Maps are supposed to tell us what the world looks like – the names, shapes and sizes of landmasses and water bodies. Though they are considered neutral depictions of land and sea, they can be sites of contention. Nations sometimes vie with one another to imprint their vision on how the landmasses they occupy, or wish to occupy, are perceived.

The map of the world that is most familiar to us is the Mercator map from the sixteenth century, named for the Flemish cartographer who created it. It has shaped our view of the world and, despite its well-known distortions, is widely used.

The Mercator map is inaccurate because it distorts the size and landmass of Africa, Latin America, South Asia and Oceania and inflates landmasses towards the poles. For example, Africa and Greenland appear to be roughly the same size, when in reality Africa is approximately 14 times larger than Greenland.

In fact, Africa is approximately 30.3 sq million – larger than the United States, China, India and much of Europe combined.

Not surprisingly, Southern nations support movements that demand equal-area geographic representations that challenge the dominant Eurocentric size distortions. The most successful campaign to date is the “Correct the Map” campaign.

For decades, Kenyans without health insurance have had one option when they fall sick, or a hospital bill arrives. Reach out to friends and family to gather what they can for their healthcare.

By 2023, official figures showed only about a quarter of Kenyans had any health cover. And most of these were people working in formal sector jobs. For the remaining 75%, who had no cover, falling sick meant paying out of their own pockets at health facilities. The few exceptions include maternity care and basic services in local clinics.

The World Health Organization estimates that half of all people worldwide impoverished by out-of-pocket health expenditures live in Africa.

In 2023, shortly after taking office, President William Ruto’s government pushed through a major health financing law, the Social Health Insurance Act. This new law scrapped the National Hospital Insurance Fund, the state insurer since 1966. The insurer had collected members’ contributions and paid their hospital bills, yet only managed to cover about a quarter of Kenyans. The new law replaced it with a new body, the Social Health Authority.

item.title: Parties skipped disclosing details of 191 candidates with criminal cases in 2026 polls: Study
item.description: The Supreme Court requires parties to explain why they chose candidates with criminal cases over those without.

Major political parties, including the Bharatiya Janata Party, Congress and Aam Aadmi Party, failed to explain why they selected 191 candidates with criminal cases for the 2026 Assembly elections as mandated by the Supreme Court, non-governmental organisation Association for Democratic Reforms said in a study on Thursday.

The candidates contested in elections in Assam, Kerala, Tamil Nadu, West Bengal and Puducherry.

item.title: ‘May hungry men learn to listen to hunger’: These new poems urge a deeper look into our beliefs
item.description: An excerpt from ‘Hymns for Longing’, by Agnibarathi.
item.content:encoded:
Hymn for Awakening

My mind is a bird
with a forked tail
fighting foes
greater than me.

I rise at dawn
and twirl and fight,
stir the overrun milk
of the day and cry in alarm.
My voice, it dons
many a cloak,
all but my own.

Pierce me, my love
with your sunbeam’s spear.
Plunder my vain clinking trinkets.

Return to me, my love,
my very own silence
and let me gaze unblinking
at your blinding glory.


Hymn for Hunting

Unwavering, my heart,
like a shikra circling distant skies
with fiery eye fixed on obscure prey
pursues you,
only you, my love.

Your waist, my love,
like a serpent that in itself
brews venom from birth and
spends it all in a single strike,
brews eternal nectar for my moment’s yen.

Like spears that fly
drawn to their foes,

like milk that flows
drawn to calves,

like seas in tumult
drawn to clouds,

my deeds, your dreams
entwined are drawn,

to death, to desire,
to us,
my love.


The Churning of a Moment’s Pleasure

Come.
Sit in my lap.
Now are our bodies one mythic mountain.

Hold.
Clasp my arms.
Now are our limbs, one cosmic serpent.

Sink.
Then rise afloat.
Now am I the turtle holding your world.

Churn. Churn. Churn.
Your gods. My demons.
My gods. Your demons.

First comes venom.

Swallow.
Hold it in our throats.
Now are we hung between life and death.

Next come treasures.

Split.
You take wealth. I take boons.
Now are we insolvent debtors forever.

At last from the shimmering ocean,
when demons become gods,
when gods become immortal, and
god becomes a seductress,

comes

nectar, nectar, nectar.

Spill.
Let life overflow and lavish.
Now have we wasted an eternity for

a moment’s pleasure.


Gossiping with a god

This afternoon,
cloistered by the bleak monsoon clouds
I invite the dancing Siva to gossip.

At my call,
he relaxes, his rigidly fluid pose,
lets the river of his hair ramble,
casts off his cool crescent moon,
lays aside his fire of wisdom,
frees the demon of ignorance,
and sits ungainly on my couch.

item.title: The 9/11 New York attacks prompted an over-reliance on security technology – leaving us vulnerable
item.description: Surveillance systems are routinely overhyped, with benefits assumed and failures routinely overlooked.
item.content:encoded:
It has been 25 years since the devastating attacks of September 11, 2001. Amid the reflection that followed emerged the most comprehensive examination of any terrorist attack in history, the 9/11 Commission Report. Several statements in this forensic diagnosis continue to shape our understanding of those events. These range from the intelligence systems that were “blinking red” in the months preceding the attacks to various institutional “failures of imagination” that left the threat unrecognised.

Yet the commission’s investigation into the circumstances of the 9/11 terrorist attacks was also, fundamentally, a report on how to reimagine and improve security. The commission’s recommendations foreshadowed and legitimised a new model of security that emerged from the ashes of the twin towers, one centred on protecting critical infrastructure using an integrated security architecture.

The 9/11 commission’s blueprint involved integrating agencies, systems and technologies. This principle took many forms. The integration of intelligence reporting is illustrated by UK’s Joint Terrorism Analysis Centre. Technology became weaved into security activities. Important spaces were fortified using a “layered security” approach.

Symbolic buildings, financial districts, city centres, stadiums, high-end shopping malls, and especially airports were the first to be upgraded. Tibet has been under Chinese control since 1951, when Tibetan leaders signed an agreement allowing Beijing to station troops in the region.

China established the Tibetan Autonomous Region in 1965. In name, this means Tibet is an autonomous region within China, but in practice it remains tightly controlled. The Tibetan government-in-exile, based in India’s Dharamshala, continues to seek independence for Tibet.

This is a continuing source of tension between India and China. New Delhi also claims part of Tibet as its own territory.

The Pune administration on Friday said it was withdrawing its order imposing a 12-day restriction on the sale and consumption of alcohol during the Hindu festival of Ganesh Chaturthi after the Bombay High Court said the blanket restriction was passed “without any rational”, Live Law reported.

The collector told the court that a fresh order will be ordered restricting the dry days to September 14, the first day of Ganesh Chaturthi, and September 25, the main immersion day, Live Law reported.

The administration had earlier imposed dry-day restrictions in parts of Pune between September 14 and September 26, citing law and order concerns during the festival, Pune Mirror reported. Some areas were to have a complete ban, while others were to observe dry days on specific festival days and along immersion procession routes.

During the hearing on Friday, a bench headed by Chief Justice Mahesh Chandra Tripathi said that such a long alcohol ban could lead to serious health problems for habitual drinkers.

“Hospitals will be flooding,” Tripathi was quoted as saying. Blanket orders without any rational cannot be allowed... You cannot say everyone who drinks will create a law and order situation.”

He added that anyone who consumed alcohol and disrupted law and order would “face the music”.
